html:
SMTO-K8S-0006 — SMTO couldn't read your Kubernetes settings file

GUID: 2130eb69-f67b-49fa-b893-aca4eb5c231b
Slug: kubernetes-config-unsupported
Domain: K8S · Subsystem: k8s

What happened

  • SMTO reads your Kubernetes settings file to note which cluster a command used, but this file is set up in a way SMTO can't read with certainty, such as repeated entries or several files at once. Your command wasn't blocked.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. If you or the agent named the Kubernetes settings file with a path starting with ~, use the full path instead, for example /home/alex/.kube/config. SMTO doesn't expand the ~ shortcut, so it can't tell which file you mean.
  2. Ask the person who manages Kubernetes access to make sure the Gateway uses one settings file, not a list of several files. When several files are combined, SMTO can't be sure which cluster entry applies.
  3. Have them remove repeated names or keys, and shortcut references between entries, from that file. Repeated entries could point to different clusters, so SMTO refuses to guess.
  4. Then ask the agent to run a read-only command such as kubectl get pods. A successful read-only command lets SMTO record the cluster from the cleaned-up file.

What success looks like

  • The read-only command succeeds and SMTO keeps using that cluster in later steps.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages Kubernetes access. Don't delete the Kubernetes settings file; it holds your sign-in for the cluster.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • Conservative kubeconfig parsing rejected the file: YAML aliases or excessive size or nesting, duplicate keys or entry names, malformed contexts/clusters/users entries, a KUBECONFIG with several files or quotes, an unresolved or ambiguous home directory, a ~ or overlong path, a document that is not apiVersion v1 kind Config, or an unsafe certificate-authority path.

What this means

  • Conservative kubeconfig parsing rejects aliases/depth/node bounds, duplicate or malformed entries, ambiguous multi-file/home selection, unsupported document structure or unsafe config/CA paths. These are local configuration/observation checks, not proof of cluster reachability or command rollback. Optional observation failure cannot change the underlying command outcome; diagnostics perform no cluster operations.

Why this can happen

  • Conservative kubeconfig parsing rejects aliases/depth/node bounds, duplicate or malformed entries, ambiguous multi-file/home selection, unsupported document structure or unsafe config/CA paths.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect the exact structural/path rejection without treating it as proof that kubectl itself is broken.

How to fix it

  • Use a single kubeconfig (KUBECONFIG set to one absolute path, or --kubeconfig with a full path), remove YAML anchors/aliases and duplicate keys or names, keep each contexts/clusters/users entry to name plus its member, and make sure the file has apiVersion: v1 and kind: Config. kubectl config view --flatten can merge several files into one supported file.
  • Inspect the indicated kubeconfig structure and duplicate keys. Use an unambiguous supported configuration or ordinary discovery; preserve private authentication data.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • Ordinary supported discovery or a valid unambiguous bounded config identifies the intended cluster.

What not to do

  • Do not bypass the unsupported-feature check or reinterpret an unsupported response as success.

Technical notes

  • These are local configuration/observation checks, not proof of cluster reachability or command rollback. Optional observation failure cannot change the underlying command outcome; diagnostics perform no cluster operations.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
